profile.summary: 2 Peter is a brief but incisive letter marked by pastoral urgency. Their focus is to encourage Christians to grow in the grace and knowledge of Christ, while warning against false teachers who try to mix the Christian faith with strange ideas of the gospel. The letter insists that Christ's return is certain, that the judgment of God is also certain and that the church must remain faithful, without yielding to moral and doctrinal deception.
profile.setting: The letter was probably addressed to the same group of Christians associated with Peter's first letter, possibly in regions of Asia Minor. The author presents himself as Simon Peter, an apostle of Jesus, but the authorship and the exact date were discussed by some interpreters, partly because of the differences in relation to 1 Peter and the similarities with Judas. The ancient Christian tradition places Peter in Rome in the early 1960s and associates his death with the period of Nero, around 64-65 AD; thus, many understand that 2 Peter would have been written shortly before that. The literary scene of the letter is of confrontation with false teachers within the community, amidst the expectation of the second coming of Christ.

structure.label: Greeting and spiritual growth
structure.description: Identification of the author and the readers, followed by the call to grow in the knowledge of God and Christ, with a personal urgency tone in the nearness of the author's death.

structure.label: Complaint of false masters
structure.description: The central section of the letter presents and condemns the false teachers, reaffirming rather the assurance of the glorious return of Christ and the judgment of God.

structure.label: Certainty of Christ's Return and Conclusion
structure.description: Peter reinforces that Christ will return and transform the world, concludes by resuming the appeal for readers to grow in the grace and knowledge of the Lord.

themes: Growth in the Grace and Knowledge of Christ
Danger of false teachers and corruption of faith
Certainty of Christ's Return and Judgment
readingKeys: Notice how the letter begins and ends with the same focus: to grow in Christ.
Read chapter 2 as the heart of the argument: the condemnation of false teachers depends on the certainty of Jesus' return.
Notice the connection between doctrine and life: the error of teaching appears along with corrupt moral practices.
profile.cautions: The authorship and date of 2 Peter are debated by scholars, and the literary relationship with Judas is also recognized, although there is no consensus on the direction of the loan. When summarizing the letter, it is important not to hurriedly identify the false masters with a specific historical group that the font does not name. The emphasis of the text is less on cataloging a heresyarch and more in warning the church against the deviation of truth and holiness.

dossier.narratedEra: The book is presented as a letter addressed to Christians of the apostolic period, amid false doctrines and expectation of Christ's return. The setting mentioned by the notes includes the life of the church in the central decades of the 1st century, with readers probably in Asia Minor and with a scenario of doctrinal controversy already underway (2Pe 1:1; 3:1).
dossier.compositionEra: The notes place the composition probably in Rome in the early 1960s, shortly before Peter's death under Nero in 64 or 65 AD. The letter is presented as Peter's second writing to the same readers of the first, and there is discussion about traditional authorship versus academic doubts: the notes state that petrine authorship is defended, but recognize that some interpreters question 2 Peter for differences in style and literary relationship with Judas. It also mentions the possibility of a different secretary in 2 Peter, in contrast to Silas/Silvano linked to 1 Peter.

politics.title: Roman Empire and the rule of Nero
politics.detail: The notes locate the tradition of Peter's death in the reign of Emperor Nero in the year 64 or 65 AD, and also mention that Peter was in Rome in the early 1960s. There is no description of internal imperial policies, but Nero's data provides the immediate political background of the composition and martirial tradition.
politics.readingImpact: The reader realizes that the letter is born in a Roman context of strong pressure on Christian leaders, which intensifies the urgent and solemn tone of Peter's warnings.

politics.title: the Apostolic Authority in Dispute
politics.detail: The notes note that the false teachers had no use for authority and that they behaved as rebels against the Lord (2 Peter 2:10-11). This is not described as a formal political system, but as a contestation of authority that directly affects ecclesial life.
politics.readingImpact: Reading gains community weight: the problem is not only moral, but also of legitimate submission to the authority of Christ and of apostolic witness.

customs.title: Community meals and Christian communion
customs.detail: The notes mention that Christians often ate together in communion meals in celebration of the Lord, and that false teachers participated in these moments to deceive or even surrender to indulge in indulgence. This is linked to the 2Pe 2:13 frame.
customs.readingImpact: The context shows that the deception was not abstract: it happened inside the community table, making the pastoral warning more concrete and painful.

customs.title: Use of Jewish and Greek names in the Greco-Roman world
customs.detail: In explaining "Simão," the notes say it was a common Jewish name and that in the Greco-Roman world, many people used both the native name and a Greek name, since Greek was the lingua franca.
customs.readingImpact: This helps to read the opening of the letter without anachronism: the name "Simon Peter" is perfectly natural for the multicultural environment of the first century.

customs.title: Spiritual family and fraternal vocation
customs.detail: The term "brothers" is explained as a Greek term that includes men and women belonging to the same family. The letter therefore speaks to a community conceived as a family of faith.
customs.readingImpact: The exhortation to perseverance and growth by virtue is not merely individual; it assumes family bonds within the church.

customs.title: Writing through Secretary
customs.detail: The introduction notes the possibility that Silas/Silvano influenced the writing of 1 Peter and that Peter may have used another secretary in 2 Peter. This is presented as plausible explanation for style differences.
customs.readingImpact: The reader is led to consider that linguistic differences do not require to automatically complete another authorship, as the practice of secretaries was part of the old composition process.

language.title: "Testamento" as a literary genre of farewell
language.detail: The notes describe 2Pe 1:12-15 as similar to the Jewish "testing" genre, in which an ancient and respected leader offers final instructions before death, with examples such as Deuteronomy 31-33 and Joshua 24.
language.readingImpact: This colores the tone of the letter: it is not only a denunciation, but also a final discourse of memory, urgency and transmission of apostolic legacy.

language.title: Structure in virtue steps
language.detail: In 2Pe 1:5-7, the sequence of virtues is explained as a literary figure called sorites, in which each trait leads to the neighbor. Notes also say that the order should not be read as rigid chronology, and that love is the apex.
language.readingImpact: Reading ceases to be a mere moral inventory; it becomes a progressive thread that culminates in love, reinforcing the formative character of the passage.

language.title: "Myth ingeniously invented"
language.detail: The expression is explained as a probable accusation of the false teachers, who treated the message about Christ's return as an uplifting fable without factual reality.
language.readingImpact: The reader understands that Peter is responding to real skepticism about parousia, and not just a generic doctrinal error.

language.title: "Day of the Lord" and "star of the morning"
language.detail: The notes explain that "Dia" is abbreviation of the Lord's day, when God intervenes to save and judge; "morning star" is associated with Venus, and the image is used in reverse: the dawn of the Lord's day leads to the brightness of the star in the hearts of believers.
language.readingImpact: The passage gains eschatological density: hope, judgment and inner illumination are articulated by cosmic and prophetic images.

language.title: Last days as a present period
language.detail: In 2Pe 3:3, the notes say that in the last days is not only pointing to a future event, but to the time that goes from the first to the second coming of Jesus. It is also said that scoffers ridicule the truth rather than seriously argue.
language.readingImpact: The context extends the scope of the warning: the situation of readers already belongs to the last days, which makes surveillance a continuous need.

timeline.title: Exited from Peter from Jerusalem around 44 A.D.
timeline.detail: The notes claim that the New Testament says little about Peter's movements after he left Jerusalem around 44 A.D., in Acts 12:16-17. This helps to frame the scarcity of data on its trajectory to Rome.
timeline.readingImpact: The reader realizes that the later tradition about Peter's career is wider than the direct biblical account, and should be treated with caution.

timeline.title: Peter in Rome in the early 1960s
timeline.detail: The introduction says that Peter was in Rome in the early 1960s and that 2 Peter was probably written from there shortly after 1 Peter.
timeline.readingImpact: This supports a reading of the letter as a late text of Peter's life, with a farewell tone and pastoral urgency.

timeline.title: Possible proximity to 1 Peter
timeline.detail: The notes understand 2 Peter as written after 1 Peter, and the phrase "this is my second letter" is treated as a reference to the previous letter, probably 1 Peter.
timeline.readingImpact: The sequence helps to interpret 2 Peter as a pastoral continuation, not as an isolated document.

timeline.title: Traditional death of Peter under Nero in 64 or 65 AD
timeline.detail: Ancient Christian tradition is mentioned as saying that Peter died under Emperor Nero in 64 or 65 AD; this serves as a backdrop for the reading of 2Pe 1:12-15 as a speech of an end of life.
timeline.readingImpact: The letter is read as a final testimony of an apostolic leader, intensifying his legacy character.

timeline.title: Literary parallels with Judas and the chronology of tradition
timeline.detail: The notes recognize an unequivocal literary relationship between 2 Peter and Judas, but do not establish an exact date for dependency. The question is presented as a debate of textual origin, not as a closed chronology.
timeline.readingImpact: The reader should read without assuming that the similarity between the letters invalidates the petrine authorship; the discussion remains open according to the source.

investigation: The source does not accurately identify false masters by name, group, or formal heresy; it only describes their immorality, pride, and skepticism.
There is no data on local governors, provincial structures or regional political conflicts in Asia Minor.

The notes mention Sodomá and Gomorrah, Noah, Lot, Balaam and the transfiguration as examples or antecedents, but these are internal biblical resources, not external historical landmarks that are damble here.
The relationship between 2 Peter and Judas is recognized as literary, but the direction of dependency continues to be debated; the source offers options, not definitive conclusion.
The hypothesis of a different secretary is presented as a possibility, not as a proven fact.
The customs appear mainly in terms of community meal, appointment, and ecclesial life; coverage on economics, work and social classes is limited.
The chronology is approximate: the source speaks in "early of the 1960s" and in 64/65 for the tradition of Peter's death, without providing exact date of composition.

This dossier is strictly limited to the notes provided and does not complete gaps with external information. Coverage is selective: there is more material about authorship, language, eschatology, and false doctrines than about imperial politics, economics, and domestic customs. Some statements are explicitly interpretative, such as the possible performance of secretaries, the reading of 2 Peter as "testance" and the relationship with Judas. Others remain debated, especially the direction of literary dependence between 2 Peter and Judas and the historical identification of the false masters. Where notes do not distinguish historical proof of theological reading, the answer preserves this distinction and indicates the nature of the data as requested.
